children.text: The Philippines' first national park, made up of 124 small limestone islands scattered across Lingayen Gulf. You can rent a bangka boat to island-hop and enjoy swimming, cave exploring, and snorkeling, which makes it a popular family getaway from Manila.

Hundred Islands National Park is a cluster of islands scattered off the coast of Alaminos City, Pangasinan, inside Lingayen Gulf in northwestern Luzon. The name means "a hundred islands," but in reality 124 islands are exposed at low tide and 123 at high tide; the park was designated the Philippines' first national park in
. The total area is about 16 km², compact enough that a bangka can take you around the main islands in an hour or two.

These islands are limestone formed from ancient coral reefs that were uplifted from the seabed over millions of years. Waves have eroded the base of many islands, leaving a wide top and a narrow "mushroom-shaped" base, with small caves and sandbars hidden in between. Most of the islands are uninhabited and covered in vegetation, with visitor facilities found only on a handful, such as Governor's, Quezon, and Children's Islands.

If you're expecting the transparent emerald water of Boracay or Palawan, you may be disappointed. Instead, its strength lies in being reachable from Manila by half a day's bus ride, and in the freedom of chartering a boat to pick and choose which islands to visit. It particularly suits families with children, groups of friends or club trips, and expats wanting a
1-night, 2-day
weekend seaside trip.
Alaminos is also known for its longganisa (Filipino sausage), and combining the trip with nearby Bolinao, Dagupan, and Manaoag makes it easy to expand into a Pangasinan loop tour.
The islands are thought to have formed about 2 million years ago when undersea coral rose above the water, and they were also declared a National Geological Monument in
. Development began after President Manuel Quezon visited Alaminos in
, and the area became a national park under Presidential Proclamation No. 667 on
January 18, 1940
; since

, the city of Alaminos has managed it directly in place of the Philippine Tourism Authority (PTA). The islands with tourist facilities are essentially Governor's, Quezon, Children's, Marcos, and Pilgrimage Islands, and a typical day of island hopping picks 4–5 of them to visit.

This island has the highest viewpoint in the park; climb the stairs for the classic view of islands large and small dotted across the sea. Go early in the morning and the island outlines stand out sharply without backlighting. A statue of St. Joseph, the patron saint of Alaminos, stands at the viewpoint, and a zipline to Virgin Island starts here.

The best-equipped island in the park, with cottages, restrooms, and a snack shop. Its gently sloping sandy beach is great for kids to play in the water, and it's the most popular lunch stop on day tours. There are a pavilion and a guesthouse, a suspension bridge links it to the neighboring island, and water activities such as helmet diving (
15 minutes
) and banana boat rides (
per person) start here too.
With shallow water and calm waves, this island suits families with children. Cottages can be rented and camping is allowed, so it also serves as an overnight camping spot.

blocks.title: Cave jumping at Imelda Cave, Marcos Island

children.text: A popular spot where you jump from a cave opening at the top of the island into the sea below. The drop is around
5m
, and you must always check the water conditions and follow the guide's instructions.

blocks.title: Snorkeling at the giant clam sanctuary

children.text: The park has a marine sanctuary where giant clams are being restored, so you can snorkel to see huge clams and small reef fish. Gear can be rented at the wharf. The park's designated snorkeling area is Old Scout Island, and you can also see giant clams below the Quezon Island boardwalk. Snorkel gear rents for
for the day, and a life vest for

Paddling yourself through the narrow channels between the islands lets you reach small caves and sandbars that are hard to get to by bangka. Mornings, when the wind is light, are best. A regular two-person kayak costs
for
1 hour
, and a clear-bottomed crystal kayak costs
for
30 minutes
; shallow Children's Island is a popular starting point.
Small, round, and strongly garlicky, Alaminos longganisa is classically eaten as "longsilog" for breakfast. Many people also buy it packaged at the market to take home as a souvenir.
An island of pilgrimage, topped by a statue of Christ the Redeemer about

tall. Climb the 263 steps along the Stations of the Cross from the beach for a sweeping view of the surrounding islands; there are two trails, a short one and a long one. The island also has a chapel, a bonsai garden, a gallery, and a coffee shop.

items.title: Taking a boat from Lucap Wharf

children.text: Tell the tricycle driver "Gonzalo Montemayor Wharf (Lucap Wharf)," and you'll be dropped off in front of the city tourist information center. Boats only run
6 AM–5:30 PM
At the counter, write down the names in your group and pay the registration fee (
per person for a day trip,
for an overnight stay). You can also create an account on the official website to register and book in advance.
Choose a boat size that fits your group and pay, and you'll be assigned a boat and a boatman. Decide which islands to visit, and in what order, together with the boatman.
Pangasinan, on Luzon's west coast, has a distinct dry and wet season.
December–May
is the dry season, when calm seas and clear skies make it the best time for island hopping;
March–May
in particular is hot enough for swimming, though the midday sun is very strong. During Holy Week and the
May
school break, Lucap Wharf gets very crowded, so an early morning start is recommended.
June–October

is the rainy season, affected by the southwest monsoon (Habagat) and typhoons. Because Lingayen Gulf opens to the west, monsoon winds raise the waves, and there are days when the coast guard bans boats from leaving. If you travel during this period, check the Alaminos tourism office's notices and the weather forecast before setting out.
November
is a transitional period when the rain starts to ease, making it an uncrowded off-peak window.

The most convenient place to stay is the Lucap waterfront in Barangay Lucap, where the wharf is located. It has a cluster of guesthouses and small hotels within walking distance of the wharf, priced at about

per night. If you want to spend a quiet night on an island, cottages and camping on Children's Island or Quezon Island can be booked at the tourist information center, though electricity and water are limited, so bring a tent, lantern, and drinking water. If you'd prefer city amenities, you can stay at a hotel in Alaminos town and take a tricycle over in the morning.

Food centers on the seafood market and grill stalls in front of Lucap Wharf. The usual approach is "paluto": you choose fish, shrimp, squid, or shellfish by weight at the market, then pay a nearby restaurant a cooking fee to have it grilled or made into soup. There are almost no restaurants on the islands, so it's a good idea to buy food before your tour and bring it along on the boat. Alaminos longganisa, grilled bangus (milkfish) from Dagupan, and the small rice cakes "puto Calasiao" from the Calasiao area are also signature foods of Pangasinan.

Along the Lucap coastal road you'll find long-established businesses registered with the city tourism office, such as Maxine by the Sea, a restaurant and inn that has been operating for over 30 years, and Island Tropic Hotel & Restaurant, where you can dine at seaside tables looking out over the islands. To spend a night on an island, book the Quezon Island guesthouse (
per night), a pavilion (
per night), or a tent site (
; tent rental

) at the tourist information center. For lunch to take on the boat, many people order a bilao set, with seafood, pancit, and longganisa arranged on a round bamboo tray, or a boodle fight set, laid out on banana leaves and shared by hand.
Bangka fares are based on group size, so if you're traveling solo, it's more economical to join other travelers at the wharf and share a boat. Ask the tourist information staff about joining a group.
Water and food on the islands are expensive or simply unavailable. Bring drinking water, snacks, and a trash bag.
Taking the first boat out at
6–7 AM
means gentler sun and quieter popular islands. Group tours crowd in after noon.
If you plan to jump at Imelda Cave or go snorkeling, a life vest is standard, and aqua shoes help protect your feet on the rocky shores.
ATMs are available in Alaminos town and along the Lucap coast, but cards and electronic payments don't work on the islands. Bring cash in small denominations.
Drone filming may require prior permission under national park rules, so check with the tourist information center first.
A waterproof pouch or bag will protect your phone and wallet from spray while riding the bangka.
Register at the tourist information center at Lucap Wharf (
6 AM–5:30 PM
); you can also book tours and view the rate table on the
official Hundred Islands National Park website
. Each group pays a garbage deposit of
, which is refunded when you bring your trash back sorted.
There is a zipline about
long on Governor's Island and about
long on Quezon Island. The fare is about
per ride, and operation sometimes stops depending on the weather.

Registration is free for children aged 5 and under, and seniors, persons with disabilities (PWD), and Pangasinan residents get a 20% discount (applied only to the environmental fee and entrance fee) on showing ID. Alaminos residents are exempt from the environmental fee.
If bad weather leads the coast guard to ban boats from leaving, island tours are suspended entirely. Build a spare day into your schedule during the rainy season.
Collecting coral or shells and taking marine life out of the national park is strictly prohibited, and violators are fined.
Cave jumping can be dangerous depending on the tide and water depth, so never jump in without a guide present.
Most islands lack shade, creating a risk of heatstroke. Bring a hat, sunscreen, and plenty of water.
Touts offering "special deal tours" outside the tourist information center's official rate card often lead to disputes over extra charges, so pay directly at the wharf counter.
After an early morning bus arrival, while it's still dark, always keep your bags and valuables close to you.
After a typhoon, operations may change while facilities are repaired. When Typhoon Emong struck on
, the park and Lucap Wharf facilities suffered about
in damage; tours did not resume until
August 1
, and overnight stays on the islands were not accepted for some time. If you plan to stay overnight on an island during the rainy season, check first whether it's operating.
